title: The Ultimate Guide to Telepresence Alternatives in 2026
summary: The best Telepresence alternatives in 2026: mirrord vs Telepresence vs Signadot compared, plus Gefyra, Telepresence pricing and support status.
body_markdown:
The main Telepresence alternatives in 2026 are mirrord, which runs a local process as if it were inside the cluster, Gefyra, which does the same for a local Docker container, and Signadot, which gives local development, every pull request and every coding agent one model: ephemeral environments on a shared cluster. mirrord and Telepresence connect one machine or process to a cluster. Signadot adds environments for every pull request and every coding agent, with databases, queues and other dependencies included.


Telepresence itself is still released as an open source project. What changed is that no company stands behind it any more, which is why many teams are looking again. For the wider field, including environment platforms, see the[comparison of Kubernetes development tools](https://www.signadot.com/blog/telepresence-mirrord-okteto-alternatives/) . For single competitors in depth, see the[Okteto alternatives](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/okteto/) and[mirrord alternatives](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/mirrord/) comparisons.

Tilt and Skaffold also show up on lists of alternatives. They rebuild and redeploy your code to a cluster on every change rather than connecting a local process, so they suit a different workflow. Both are active.


## What Telepresence does in Kubernetes, and what changed


Telepresence connects a developer’s machine to a Kubernetes cluster. A service running on your laptop can call cluster services by their DNS names, and traffic meant for a workload in the cluster can be sent to your laptop instead. It is a[CNCF Sandbox project](https://www.cncf.io/projects/telepresence/) , accepted in 2018 and originally created by Ambassador Labs.


### How Telepresence works


According to the[Telepresence architecture docs](https://telepresence.io/docs/concepts/architecture) , three parts work together:


- **A Traffic Manager** runs once in the cluster, usually installed by an administrator.
- **A traffic agent** attaches to the workload you work on, injected as a sidecar or, since version 2.30, through an optional node agent that does not restart pods.
- **Daemons on your machine** create a virtual network interface and DNS resolver. The root daemon asks for administrator rights unless you install from a package or use the` --docker` mode.


It has[four ways to attach](https://telepresence.io/docs/concepts/attachments) to a workload:` intercept` sends the workload’s traffic to your machine while the remote container keeps running,` replace` swaps the container out entirely,` wiretap` sends you a read-only copy of the traffic, and` ingest` gives you the workload’s environment and volumes without any traffic. Since version 2.25, open source Telepresence can filter an intercept by HTTP header or path, so several developers can work on the same service at once.


Two friction points remain: the virtual network interface can conflict with corporate VPNs, and every developer needs their own credentials for the cluster.


### Telepresence pricing and status in 2026


Telepresence is free and open source under the Apache 2.0 license, and the project is busy. Version 2.32.2[shipped on October 8, 2026](https://github.com/telepresenceio/telepresence/releases) , with releases every two to four weeks through the year.


The commercial story is what changed. Ambassador moved its paid Telepresence features into its Blackbird platform in early 2025, then[Gravitee acquired Ambassador in July 2025](https://www.gravitee.io/blog/ambassador-labs-gravitee-what-our-acquisition-means-for-you) . As of October 2026, the old getambassador.io product pages redirect to Gravitee, Gravitee does not offer Blackbird or a paid Telepresence, and no company sells support or an SLA for it. The project is kept up mostly by one maintainer, who wrote about 90% of the commits since April, and its only sponsor[ended its sponsorship](https://github.com/telepresenceio/telepresence/discussions/4334) on October 7, 2026. Help comes from GitHub and the CNCF Slack. Teams that need a vendor behind their tooling are the ones looking hardest at alternatives.

These are the three tools buyers compare most. The table covers the questions that usually decide it.

The short version: mirrord and Telepresence connect one process or machine to a cluster. Signadot gives local development, pull requests and coding agents one model, the ephemeral environment, with databases, queues and other dependencies in it, so the environment you develop in is the one your pull request and tests use.


### mirrord vs Telepresence


The two tools solve the same problem in different ways.


- **Mechanism.** Telepresence creates a virtual network interface on your machine, so everything on the machine can reach the cluster.[mirrord loads a library into one process](https://metalbear.com/mirrord/docs/reference/architecture) and hooks its network and file calls, so only that process is connected. That is why mirrord usually needs less setup and conflicts less with corporate VPNs.
- **Default behavior.** mirrord mirrors incoming traffic by default and only takes it over when you ask. Telepresence intercepts by default, and added a read-only` wiretap` mode in 2025, so this is no longer a difference in capability, only in defaults.
- **Sharing a cluster.** Both can filter traffic by HTTP header so several developers work on one service. In Telepresence this is free. In mirrord, concurrent use of one service needs the Team plan.
- **Data and queues.** mirrord’s paid plans add[database branching](https://metalbear.com/mirrord/docs/sharing-the-cluster/db-branching) and[queue splitting](https://metalbear.com/mirrord/docs/sharing-the-cluster/queue-splitting) . Telepresence has neither.
- **Beyond the laptop.** mirrord offers CI runs and preview environments on Enterprise. Telepresence stays a developer tool.
- **Price.** Telepresence is free. mirrord is free for individuals and $50 per seat per month for teams.


So Telepresence vs mirrord comes down to setup and budget. If you want a free tool and are comfortable with the networking setup, Telepresence is fine. If you want the lowest-friction local workflow and will pay for team features, mirrord is the stronger choice. If you are looking for a mirrord alternative because you need an environment for every pull request rather than a faster local loop, the[mirrord alternative comparison](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/mirrord/) covers where each tool fits, and[Signadot vs Telepresence](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/telepresence/) does the same for Telepresence.


## The other local-to-cluster tools


### Gefyra


[Gefyra](https://gefyra.dev/) runs your code in a local Docker container attached to the cluster network over WireGuard. Your container can call cluster services as if it were a pod. To receive cluster traffic, Gefyra’s bridge[patches the target workload](https://gefyra.dev/en/information/run-vs-bridge) and routes requests to your container. Since version 2.4, personal bridges match on HTTP headers or paths, so developers can share a workload.


Gefyra is free, open source and maintained, with version 2.5.6 released on October 6, 2026. The catch is the container requirement: if you prefer to run processes directly on your machine, mirrord or Telepresence fit better. Its Docker Desktop extension still runs the older Gefyra 1.


### Retired and slowing tools


Some tools that appear on older lists of Telepresence alternatives are gone or fading:


- **Bridge to Kubernetes** from Microsoft was[retired on April 30, 2025](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/bridge/overview-bridge-to-kubernetes) . Microsoft named mirrord and Telepresence as replacements.
- **ksync** is archived on GitHub, and **kt-connect** has not had a release since 2022.
- **Okteto Cloud** , the free hosted tier, closed on January 15, 2024. Okteto itself is active as a self-hosted platform, covered in the[Okteto alternatives comparison](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/okteto/) .
- **DevSpace** is still a CNCF Sandbox project, but its last stable release was in April 2026 and activity has slowed.


## Signadot: ephemeral environments for every change


Signadot is not a tunnel. It gives every pull request, developer and coding agent an ephemeral environment on a shared Kubernetes cluster, and it covers the local workflow the tools above are known for as one way of using that environment.


**How it works.** The stable version of every service runs once in the cluster. For each change, Signadot duplicates only the services and components that need isolating, usually just the changed services, and plugs them into the rest of the shared environment. It links them in three ways: request routing for synchronous traffic, message routing for asynchronous and batch work, and configuration changes that point a service at a new version. How much each change duplicates is up to you, from one service to the whole stack. Because so little is copied, environments start in seconds. Request routing runs through the mesh you already have. On Istio, Signadot updates your VirtualService rules and Istio’s own sidecars or ambient mode do the routing, with no extra sidecar. It also works with the Gateway API, and with Linkerd or no mesh a lightweight DevMesh sidecar routes requests.


**Data and dependencies.** This is where Signadot differs most from the local-to-cluster tools.


- **Databases.** A change can share a database, or get its own through a[resource plugin](https://www.signadot.com/docs/concepts/resources) or a branching provider such as[Neon](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/set-up-data-isolation) . The plugin creates the resource with the environment and deletes it afterwards.
- **Message queues.** Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SQS and Pub/Sub stay shared. Producers tag messages with the environment’s routing key, and a[routing API and libraries](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/set-up-message-queue-isolation) tell each consumer which messages are its own.
- **Workflow engines.** The same approach works for[Temporal workers on a shared task queue](https://www.signadot.com/docs/tutorials/testing-temporal-workers) .
- **Resources outside Kubernetes.** Resource plugins can create and delete managed databases, queues, buckets and other cloud resources with each environment, written with Helm, Terraform or a cloud CLI.


**Local development.** With[local development](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/use-cases/set-up-local-testing) , you run the service you are changing on your machine. Requests in the cluster that carry your environment’s routing key reach your local process, and your process reaches cluster services, databases and queues by their usual Kubernetes DNS names. Many developers share one cluster without stepping on each other.


**Pull requests and tests.** CI[creates an environment for every pull request](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/set-up-pr-sandboxes) in seconds. Your existing tests run against it, from CI or inside the cluster as[Jobs](https://www.signadot.com/docs/concepts/smart-tests-and-jobs) , and[RouteGroups](https://www.signadot.com/docs/reference/route-groups) combine environments when a feature spans several services and pull requests.


**Deployment model.** Signadot is hybrid. The operator runs in your cluster, with a thin SaaS control plane. By default the control plane receives only resource metadata, such as workload names, namespaces, image references and status, never source code, image contents or application data. Signadot runs in pre-production, so it does not see production PII. Opt-in features such as Smart Diff traffic capture and Job logs send more, encrypted at rest. Signadot is SOC 2 Type II, and the[data and integrations page](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/admin/security/data-integrations) has the details.


Other environment platforms take a different route. Release and Bunnyshell give each environment a copy of the application, and so does Okteto by default, though its Divert feature can share services from another namespace. Full copies work well for smaller stacks and get expensive as the number of services grows. The[Okteto alternatives](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/okteto/) and[Release (ReleaseHub) alternative](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/release/) pages compare those approaches.


## What coding agents change


Coding agents change who needs an environment, and how many need one at once. The[CircleCI 2026 State of Software Delivery report](https://www.signadot.com/blog/circleci-2026-report-agent-validation-gap/) found that average throughput grew 59% year over year, while roughly 30% of merge attempts now fail and median recovery takes 72 minutes. A 50-engineer team built for 100 to 150 pull requests a day is now[looking at 1,000](https://www.signadot.com/blog/the-agent-pr-flood-is-here-if-you-run-istio-youre-halfway-to-solving-it/) .


Local-to-cluster tools were designed around one person at one workstation. That shows up in three ways once agents do part of the work.


1. **Agents run where there is no laptop.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot’s coding agent increasingly run in cloud sessions and CI runners. A tool whose main workflow is a daemon or a process on a developer’s machine has to be adapted to run there.
2. **Agents run in parallel.** One developer may have four agent sessions open, each changing a different service or the same service in different ways. Each needs its own isolated copy of the change, its own data where the change touches a schema, and its own routing so that one agent’s test traffic never reaches another agent’s code.
3. **Agents need a closed loop.** An agent can only fix what it can observe. It needs to create an environment, run the tests or requests that exercise its change, read the result and try again, without asking a human to open a tunnel.


Local development is turning into agentic development: most code is now written by an agent, on a laptop or in the cloud. All three tools now have something for agents. Telepresence has a built-in MCP server, and mirrord ships agent skills and offers cloud agents on Enterprise. Both still center on connecting one machine to a cluster. Signadot gives each agent run its own ephemeral environment through its[MCP server](https://www.signadot.com/docs/integrations/mcp) and[agent skills](https://www.signadot.com/docs/integrations/coding-agents/agent-skills) , with only the agent’s changes duplicated, so dozens of agents can test against the same cluster at once. That includes background agents running in cloud sandboxes, as in our[Modal example](https://github.com/signadot/examples/tree/main/modal-sandboxes-tutorial) . The agent and your tests do the checking. Signadot provides the environment they check in. The guide to[validating AI-generated code on Kubernetes](https://www.signadot.com/validate-ai-generated-code-kubernetes/) covers the full loop.


## How to choose


**Stay on Telepresence when** it already works for your team, you want a free open source tool, community support is enough, and your need is one developer at a time debugging a service against a cluster.


**Choose mirrord when** one developer at a time needs a quick link from a laptop process to a cluster. Pay for the Team plan if several developers share a cluster or need database branching and queue splitting.


**Choose Gefyra when** your team already develops inside Docker containers and wants a free, container-based workflow.


**Choose Signadot when** you need an environment for every pull request and coding agent, your changes touch databases, queues or workflow engines such as Temporal, or many developers and agents must test on one cluster at the same time. Local development, pull requests and coding agents share one model, the ephemeral environment, so Signadot replaces a local-to-cluster tool rather than sitting beside it. Need fully self-hosted?[Talk to us](https://www.signadot.com/schedule-a-call/) .


## Moving off Telepresence


Signadot’s routing relies on the same thing Telepresence’s header-based intercepts need: each service passes a header such as W3C` baggage` on to the services it calls. Teams that already use personal intercepts usually have that in place. The[technical guide to migrating from Telepresence to Signadot](https://www.signadot.com/blog/how-to-migrate-from-telepresence-to-signadot-a-technical-guide/) walks through the one-time setup, moving the local workflow over, adding pull request environments, and how Telepresence concepts map to Signadot ones.


## Frequently asked questions


What is the best alternative to Telepresence?


The like-for-like swaps are mirrord, which runs a local process as if it were inside the cluster without a VPN-style tunnel, and Gefyra, which does the same for a local Docker container. Signadot goes further with one model, the ephemeral environment, for local development, every pull request and every coding agent, with databases and queues isolated per change. The environment you or your agent develop in is the one your pull request and tests use.


mirrord vs Telepresence: which is better?


Both connect a local process to a Kubernetes cluster and both are actively maintained. mirrord is usually quicker to set up because it hooks the process's network and file calls instead of creating a network interface, and its paid tiers add database branching, queue splitting and preview environments. Telepresence is free and open source, a CNCF Sandbox project, with header-based personal intercepts and a built-in MCP server. Pick by setup friction and whether you will pay for team features.


What are the best alternatives to mirrord?


Telepresence and Gefyra are the like-for-like alternatives to mirrord: all three connect a locally running process or container to a remote Kubernetes cluster. Signadot is the alternative when you need more than the inner loop: an ephemeral environment for every pull request and coding agent, with databases, message queues and Temporal workflows isolated per change. Signadot's mirrord comparison page covers the two side by side.


Is Telepresence still maintained?


The code is, but no company supports it. Version 2.32.2 shipped on October 8, 2026, and it remains a CNCF Sandbox project. Ambassador Labs moved its paid Telepresence features into Blackbird, Gravitee bought Ambassador in July 2025, and today no one sells support or an SLA. Most recent work comes from one maintainer, and the project's only sponsor ended its sponsorship in October 2026.


How much does Telepresence cost?


Telepresence is free and open source under the Apache 2.0 license. As of October 2026 no paid Telepresence tier is offered: the commercial features moved into Ambassador's Blackbird platform, and Gravitee, which acquired Ambassador in July 2025, does not market either one. For comparison, mirrord's Team plan costs $50 per seat per month, and Signadot has a free Starter plan and usage-based paid plans.


What does Telepresence do in Kubernetes?


Telepresence connects your workstation to a Kubernetes cluster so a service running on your laptop can call cluster services by their DNS names and receive traffic meant for a workload in the cluster. A Traffic Manager runs in the cluster, a traffic agent attaches to the workload, and daemons on your machine create a virtual network interface. Modes include intercept, replace, wiretap and ingest.


Can coding agents use Telepresence or mirrord?


Partly. Telepresence has a built-in MCP server that Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code can use to drive it, and mirrord ships agent skills for Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode. Both still center on one machine connected to a cluster. Agents running many tasks in parallel, on laptops or as background agents in the cloud, need an environment per task, which Signadot creates through its MCP server and agent skills, with only the agent's changes duplicated.


Does Signadot support local development like Telepresence does?


Yes. With Signadot you run the service you are changing on your machine inside an ephemeral environment. Requests in the cluster that carry your environment's routing key reach your local process, and your process reaches the cluster's real services, databases and queues by their Kubernetes DNS names. Many developers share the same cluster without interfering, and the same environment then serves pull request previews and coding agents.
